title: The Stolen Volkswagen on Cervantes Street
description: A routine plate check behind a closed Pensacola restaurant leads a young officer to arrest a man who gives a false name, and two days later that name turns out to be Ted Bundy. The investigator who spent forty hours interrogating him recounts what Bundy confessed, and explains why he's refused to take part in any film made about that night since.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: It's one in the morning on the fifteenth of February, 1978, on Cervantes Street in Pensacola, Florida, a wide road of fast food places and empty lots on the western edge of the city. An orange Volkswagen Beetle is sitting in the parking lot behind Oscar Woerner's restaurant, which is closed and dark. Officer David Lee is driving through the area on patrol. There's nothing dramatic about the moment. Just a car sitting where it shouldn't be, at an hour when almost nobody is around. Lee watches as the Volkswagen pulls out onto Cervantes. He follows it, runs the plate, and gets a hit. The car has been reported stolen. Lee pulls it over near W Street and Cross Street and orders the driver out. The man gives him a false name. Then, as Lee tries to handcuff him, the man fights back. He strikes the officer, breaks free, and runs. Lee draws his weapon and fires, but the man keeps going. Lee catches him and eventually gets him into custody. At the station, the prisoner is booked under the name Kenneth Misner. For the moment, that's who the police think they have. The investigator assigned to the case is Norman Chapman. And Chapman doesn't recognize the man sitting in front of him. Hours later, after the questioning has begun, the prisoner finally gives them his real name. Theodore Robert Bundy. The name means almost nothing to Chapman. But outside Pensacola, Bundy is already one of the most wanted men in America. And the strangest part is how close the police came to never knowing who they had arrested at all. According to Norman Chapman, Bundy had already been driving toward Mobile when he turned back into Pensacola, saying he felt the urge to find another victim. He stopped behind Oscar's Restaurant and began peeping into nearby homes. Whatever he was looking for that night, he never got the chance to find it.

turns.speaker: narrator
turns.text: Chapman would spend roughly forty hours talking to Bundy, alongside other investigators, trying to understand the man they had accidentally caught. And Bundy eventually said something that Chapman would remember for the rest of his life. He said he couldn't go to anyone with his problem. He couldn't sit down with a psychiatrist and explain what was wrong with him. Because the problem, as Bundy put it, was that he killed people. By then, investigators were beginning to connect him to the murders of two Florida State University students and to the disappearance of twelve-year-old Kimberly Leach. Bundy was eventually convicted of the Leach murder and sentenced to death. He was executed in Florida's electric chair on January 24th, 1989. Norman Chapman went on to become chief of the Pensacola Police Department. And decades later, he watched Hollywood keep returning to the story of Ted Bundy. Chapman wanted little to do with it. He had turned down involvement with films about Bundy, including the 2019 film starring Zac Efron. His objection was simple: Hollywood had to create drama around events that, to him, were already dramatic enough. Because Chapman remembered what the cameras couldn't recreate. It wasn't a dark interrogation room or a carefully planned manhunt. It was a quiet road in Pensacola, an orange Volkswagen, a routine patrol, and one police officer who happened to look twice. A few minutes earlier, Bundy was still free. A few minutes later, the most notorious serial killer in America was sitting in a police station, and the man who caught him didn't even know his name.
